question: Neuroanatomy What structure sits in the sella turcica and what bone makes up the sella turcica?

options.A: the optic chiasm; the temporal bone
options.B: the optic chiasm; the sphenoid bone
options.C: the pituitary gland; the temporal bone
options.D: the pituitary gland; the sphenoid bone

explanation: The optic chiasm sits approximately 10 mm superior to the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone where the pituitary gland sits. Clinically, this is important because a pituitary adenoma must typically reach a minimum size of 1 cm to threaten compression of the optic chiasm above.

question: Neurosurgeons perform a craniotomy and resect the anterior half of the right temporal lobe due to uncontrollable temporal lobe seizures. What visual consequences might be expected as a result of this surgery?

options.A: a left hemianopia in the right eye only
options.B: loss of visual acuity in the right eye only
options.C: a left inferior quadrantanopia in both eyes
options.D: a left superior quadrantanopia in both eyes

explanation: Visual information for the left side of the visual field in both eyes exits the optic chiasm and synapses in the right lateral geniculate nucleus. This information then passes from the right lateral geniculate nucleus to the right primary visual area of the occipital lobe (Brodmann area 17) by way of the optic radiations. Visual information (in the optic radiations) which correspond to the left superior quadrant of the visual field in both eyes passes through the right temporal lobe in a pathway called the loop of Meyer. Meanwhile, visual information (in the optic radiations) for the left inferior quadrant of the visual field in both eyes passes through the parietal lobe. The clinical significance of this complicated pathway is that a lesion of the right temporal lobe results in loss of the left superior quadrant of the visual field in both eyes (also known as a left homonymous superior quadrantanopia). What is the total volume of the orbit? A.1 cc B.10 cc C.30 cc D.100 cc High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The orbit measures approximately 45 mm wide and 35 mm in maximal height. The total volume is approximately 30 cc. The optic canal transmits the optic nerve from the orbit into the intracranial cavity. The optic canal passes through which bone? A.palatine B.sphenoid C.maxillary D.frontal High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: The optic nerve passes through the optic canal of the sphenoid bone to exit the orbit. Of note the optic canal is formed by the lesser (not greater) wing of the sphenoid (high yield). The optic canal is thought to be the location of injury in traumatic optic neuropathy. Other structures which pass through the optic canal include the ophthalmic artery and the sympathetic nerves traveling to the eye. Neurosurgeons often remove pituitary adenomas endoscopically via the sphenoid sinus. What key structure is in danger of damage during this procedure? A.the infraorbital nerve B.the infraorbital artery C.the inferior rectus muscle D.the optic nerve High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The optic nerve exits the orbit via the optic canal. The medial wall of the optic canal is separated from the sphenoid sinus by a very thin plate of sphenoid bone. Entering the sphenoid sinus to gain access to the pituitary gland can be complicated by damage to the adjacent optic nerve. Approximately how many ganglion cell axons combine to form the optic nerve? A.1.2 million B.6 million C.10 million D.100 million High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This question is one that should be committed to memory. There are approximately 1-1.2 million ganglion cells which make up the optic nerve. What are the average diameters of the optic nerve head and intraorbital optic nerve respectively? A.1 mm; 2 mm B.1.5 mm; 3 mm C.3 mm; 6 mm D.1 cm; 2 cm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Like many anatomy questions, this fact must just be memorized. The average optic nerve head measures 1.5 mm in diameter. As the ganglion cell axons exits the globe via the lamina cribosa and becomes myelinated by oligodendrocytes, the optic nerve size doubles to 3 mm in diameter.

question: which of the following MRI sequences attenuates the otherwise bright cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal thus making it the ideal sequence for evaluation of periventricular white matter changes in patients with multiple sclerosis?
explanation: T1 weighted images provide the best visualization of anatomy. In T1 images, fat is bright while CSF, vitreous, and air is dark. T2 images optimize the difference in water content between tissues and therefore is excellent for demonstrating pathology. In T2 images, fat is less bright than in T1, and CSF / aqueous is very bright. Bone is tricky because it depends on the location and type of bone. Compact bone without marrow is dark on T1 and T2 but bone with prominent bone marrow (which includes the adult calvarium) will be bright on T1 and somewhat bright on T2 due to fat content. FLAIR (or fluid attenuated inversion recovery) is a subset of T2 sequencing that attenuates the bright signal of CSF allowing for better visualization in the periventricular regions adjacent to the CSF. DWI (or diffusion weighted imaging) is a sequence which highlights recent vascular perfusion abnormalities. Thus, DWI is ideal for evaluation of cerebral infarctions. DWI can show a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) minutes after onset and will stay abnormal up to 3 weeks following a CVA.

options.A: 23-year-old involved in a motor vehicle accident with double vision and periocular swelling in the right eye
options.B: 40-year-old female with acute monocular vision loss and eye pain worse with eye movement
options.C: 60-year-old with an acute onset internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) on clinical exam
options.D: 4-year-old with a 2 month history of ataxia and running into objects

explanation: MRI is preferable to CT for most non-urgent ophthalmic complaints because of its excellent visualization of the cerebrum, brainstem, orbital apex and structures near the skull base. MRI also does not subject patients to ionizing radiation and the contrast agent is generally considered safer than the nephrotoxic IV contrast used with CT. Situations where CT is preferable include trauma and other clinical scenarios where hemorrhage and bony structures need to be assessed. CT is considerably faster than MRI which also makes it preferable in urgent trauma situations when images are needed quickly and the patient may not be capable of staying still for a prolonged period of time. Patients suspicious for optic neuritis should always be evaluated with MRI of the brain and orbits to assess both for optic neuritis and other multiple sclerosis type plaques in the brain. An INO localizes to pathology in the brainstem which is best visualized with a MRI. When possible, MRI is preferable in children to avoid ionizing radiation exposure. A 40-year old Caucasian female presents with acute vision loss in the right eye associated with eye pain worse with eye movement. On exam the patient has 20/60 best corrected vision in the right eye and 20/20 vision in the left eye. She demonstrates an afferent pupillary defect and difficulty with color vision in the right eye. Which of the following tests is the most important to assess her long-term prognosis for development of multiple sclerosis? A.Detailed family history B.Visual field test to assess for any deficits in the contralateral eye C.MRI of the brain to look for white matter lesions D.MRI of the orbits with IV contrast to confirm enhancement of the right optic nerve High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) showed that the long-term risk for development of multiple sclerosis (MS) can be assessed in patients with isolated optic neuritis based on the presence or absence of characteristic white matter changes on MRI of the brain. A patient with isolated optic neuritis and no characteristic white matter changes on MRI of the brain has a 22% risk of MS development in 10 years. This risk climbs to 56% in 10 years for patients with one or more white matter lesions. The 10-year risk for MS development among all patients with a single bout of clinically isolated optic neuritis (not taking into account MRI findings) is 38%. This information can be remembered as the "10/20/40/60 rule." MRI of the orbits is often performed in patients with atypical presentations of optic neuritis, but is not necessary for the clinical diagnosis of optic neuritis and has no bearing on prognosis for development of MS. Assessment for subclinical involvement of the contralateral eye in a patient with apparent monocular optic neuritis likewise does not aid in prediction of MS formation. ------------ More information regarding the ONTT findings (15-year data): The ONTT enrolled patients between 1988 and 1991 and followed them prospectively for 15 years. The 15-year data found the following: • The probability of developing MS by 15 years after an episode of optic neuritis was 50%. • If no lesions were found on baseline brain MRI, then the risk was 25% over 15 years. • If one or more lesions were found on baseline brain MRI, then the risk was 72% over 15 years. Optic Neuritis Study Group. Multiple sclerosis risk after optic neuritis: final optic neuritis treatment trial follow-up. Arch Neurol. 2008;65:727-32. A 25-year old obese female with properly-diagnosed idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) has severe daily headaches for the last year, mild optic disc edema, and 20/20 central visual acuity OU. Three serial Humphrey visual fields (24-2) show only enlargement of the blind spot. She has seen three headache specialists and tried numerous unsuccessful treatments including over-the-counter NSAIDs, acetazolamide, topiramate, nortriptyline, and several 1-week courses of prednisone. Her headaches did improve for 12-24 hours following two different diagnostic lumbar punctures. What is the next best step in management of this patient? A.optic nerve sheath fenestration of both eyes B.neurosurgical referral for possible lumboperitoneal shunt C.serial high volume lumbar punctures D.long-term prednisone therapy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: The indications for surgical intervention in idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) include progressive visual loss and/or intractable headaches despite maximal medical therapy. Optic nerve sheath fenestration is the preferred procedure in cases with progressive visual loss. The fenestrations scar quickly, unfortunately, leading to a 15% success rate at 6 years. When intractable headache is the predominant symptom, lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal shunts are the procedures of choice. These shunts are successful in relieving headache but have a high complication rate. Subsequent shunt revisions are required in approximately 50%. Serial "therapeutic" large volume lumbar taps were utilized in the past for treatment of IIH but this is no longer an accepted treatment of IIH. Long-term prednisone is unlikely to be effective for chronic IIH-related headache and has numerous serious side-effects. A 75-year old female comes in with vague chronically progressive visual complaints. Despite good uncorrected visual acuity (20/25) in both eyes, she claims that she can't see well and her husband states that she doesn't seem to understand what she sees. A mini-mental status exam reveals difficulty with concentration and short-term memory. The patient has difficulty with visuospatial tasks such as drawing a clock face. You suspect that she may suffer from the visual variant of Alzheimer's disease (VVAD). A recent MRI was unremarkable except for mild diffuse cortical atrophy. What would be the most helpful next test? A.CT of the brain with IV contrast B.magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) C.functional MRI (fMRI) D.computerized tomographic angiography (CTA) High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: The visual variant of Alzheimer's disease (or posterior cortical atrophy) is usually a slowly progressive variant of Alzheimer's degeneration that predominately affects the parietal and occipital lobes early in the disease course resulting in difficulty with visuospatial tasks and vague visual complaints (often despite good visual acuity). Over time, it usually generalizes and results in memory deficits and cognitive decline similar to standard Alzheimer's disease. Often neuro- imaging studies such as CT and MRI are unremarkable but the diagnosis can be confirmed on fMRI (functional MRI), PET scanning (positron emission tomography), or SPECT testing (single photon emission tomography). All three of these studies (fMRI, PET,and SPECT) are tests of physiologic function used to highlight areas of hypometabolism and/or hypoperfusion in the brain. In this case of VVAD, a fMRI would be expected to show focal hypoperfusion / hypometabolism of the occipital-parietal region. A 60-year old female underwent pituitary adenoma resection 2 years ago followed immediately by brain radiation. She now presents with a 2 month history of episodes of intermittent binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia. On exam she has 20/25 visual acuity in both eyes but demonstrates intermittent spasm of the right medial rectus and right inferior rectus lasting anywhere from 15 seconds to 2 minutes. A follow-up MRI of the brain shows chronic changes related to her prior tumor resection and radiation but no other pathology. What is the best next step in this patient? A.perform a Tensilon (edrophonium) test B.strabismus surgery C.psychiatry consultation for a functional disorder D.a trial of carbamazepine therapy High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: This patient underwent prior brain radiation which very rarely can be complicated by ocular neuromyotonia months to years later. Ocular neuromyotonia results in spasms of some or all muscles supplied by cranial nerves 3, 4, or 6 (in this case CN 3) resulting in episodic binocular diplopia lasting seconds to minutes. It is thought that this is due to tonic discharges of the offending cranial nerve related to some sort of prior insult (radiation, surgery, etc). In the majority of cases there is a history of prior radiation treatment. Fortunately, most cases of ocular neuromyotonia improve significantly with carbamazepine therapy.

explanation: This coronal slice of a T1-weighted post-contrast MRI shows a large pituitary mass consistent with a pituitary adenoma expanding superiorly to compress the chiasm. Pituitary masses classically compress the middle portion of the inferior optic chiasm (white arrow). The retinal ganglion cell axons first compromised by such compression would be the inferonasal fibers supplying the superotemporal visual fields in both eyes. With increasing compression more fibers become involved and the deficits may progress to a complete hemianopia. Which of the following clinical presentations does NOT require neuro-imaging? A.a 30-year old with a newly-discovered bitemporal hemianopia B.a 60-year old hypertensive with an acute painless inferior altitudinal field defect OD with associated afferent pupillary defect and disc edema OD. C.a 60-year old hypertensive with ptosis, dilated pupil, and limitation of upgaze and adduction OD. D.a 50-year old with chronic blurring OD and an associated pale nerve with an afferent pupillary defect OD. High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Neuro-imaging in vasculopathic patients presenting with typical NAION (non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy) is virtually always unremarkable and therefore not necessary. Newly- discovered APDs with nerve pallor always warrant neuro-imaging evaluation to rule out compressive lesions. Any newly-discovered visual field disturbance suggestive of retrochiasmal pathology (respecting the vertical midline) also requires neuro-imaging. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy is always considered to be due to a PCOM aneurysm until proven otherwise (with non-invasive MRA, non-invasive CTA, or invasive conventional angiography).

question: in the coronal cut of the T1-weighted post-contrast MRI shown above, what structure does the tip of arrow "A" touch?
explanation: Even if you hate neuro-anatomy, you should take 5 minutes to memorize the midline structures of the brain. Arrow A points to the “intracavernous” portion of the right internal carotid artery. Because of the loop and posterior turn that the internal carotid artery makes after passing anteriorly through the cavernous sinus, a coronal section through the cavernous sinus often shows two lumens of the internal carotid artery in the same section (in this image the dark circle above arrow A is also the right internal carotid artery). Because the internal carotid artery runs in the cavernous sinus, a rupture or leak of the intracavernous internal carotid artery causes a “direct” or “high flow” carotid cavernous fistula. The exam findings in these patients is often very dramatic including severe proptosis, diffuse ophthalmoplegia, central retinal vein occlusion, and major arterialization of the conjunctival vessels. Arrow B shows the left optic nerve as it enters the chiasm. Arrow C is pointing towards the pituitary gland overlying the sphenoid sinus (arrow D). A 45-year old hypertensive, diabetic female presents acutely with a pupil-involving cranial nerve 3 (CN III) palsy. Which of the following tests appropriate in the evaluation of cerebral aneurysm has the highest morbidity? A.Catheter angiography B.Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) C.Computerized tomographic angiography (CTA) D.There is no test necessary in this situation High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Pupil-involving CN III palsy is always considered to be due to an aneurysm of the posterior communicating (PCOM) artery until proven otherwise. Typically a MRA or CTA test is performed first because they are non-invasive and, aside from rare intravenous contrast complications, are considered very safe. Catheter angiography (aka conventional or contrast angiography) is the gold standard for aneurysm detection but is an invasive test with a 1-2.5% morbidity rate (mostly due to the risk of ischemia from emboli or vasospasm).

explanation: The patient is presenting with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON). LHON causes a sequential acute or subacute failure of vision in both eyes with the average interval between the first and second eye being two to three months. Vision loss is typically painless, although headaches occasionally occur and Uhthoff’s phenomena (worsening of vision associated with elevation of body temperature) has been reported. Visual acuity reflects the dense central scotoma that develops and typically ranges between 20/800 and 20/200, but only rarely leads to hand motion or light perception levels of vision. Initially, in the second uninvolved eye, mild subclinical central visual field abnormalities can be seen on formal visual field testing. An afferent pupillary defect may or may not be present. On fundoscopic examination, pseudoswelling of the optic nerve with telangiectatic capillaries is the classic appearance. On fluorescein angiography, there is no leakage of the swollen disc and eventually disc atrophy ensues. In this case, the ganglion cell analysis shows diffuse atrophy of the right nerve with an initial area of thinning of the left nerve. The right optic nerve has temporal pallor compared to the left. LHON is due to a mitochondrial DNA mutation that results in disruption of oxidative phosphorylation due to an excess of reactive oxidative species. The most common mutation is at the 11778 position, followed by the 3460 or 14484 positions. Patients with the 14484 mutation have the greatest chance of spontaneous recovery. As a mitochondrially inherited disease, the mother can only transmit the disease. The disease is characterized by marked incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity with 80-90% of all affected patients being male. Current treatments aim at reducing oxidative stress on the mitochondria and includes idebenone (an analog of coenzyme Q10) and counseling patients on smoking and alcohol cessation. WRONG ANSWERS: (Choice A) As a mitochondrially inherited disease, LHON can only be transmitted from the mother. Additionally, for debated reasons, 80-90% of affected individuals are male. (Choice B) The disease is mitochondrially inherited, not autosomal dominant. Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA), also known as Kjer’s optic neuropathy, is the most commonly inherited optic neuropathy. ADOA presents in the first decade of life with slowly progressive bilateral vision loss typically detected on school screenings. Patients usually retain 20/200 vision or better. (Choice C): Differential diagnosis of LHON includes nonhereditary optic neuropathies (e.g., infiltrative, compressive, or toxic/metabolic etiologies) and optic neuritis and testing can exclude other causes. MRI imaging in LHON can show optic nerve enhancement in the acute phase as well T2 hyperintensity that may involve both optic nerves simultaneously as well as the chiasm prior to the second eye involvement. A 14-year-old female is referred in for papilledema noted on routine eye exam. Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally, there is no relative afferent pupillary defect, and color vision is full. The disc appearance and autofluorescence findings are similar in both eyes. What other ancillary test is most likely to support the diagnosis suggested by the images above? A.B Scan ultrasonography B.MRI Brain C.Lumbar puncture with opening pressure D.OCT Macula High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The patient in this case has pseudopapilledema due to optic disc drusen (ODD). Optic disc drusen (ODD) are refractile, often calcified nodules within the optic nerve head. They are bilateral in most cases (75-86%), which can make distinguishing them from true papilledema quite challenging at times. The disc margin is often blurred in cases of ODD due to axoplasmic stasis in the axons deep within the optic nerve head. However, unlike in true papilledema, there is no RNFL edema and therefore the view of the retinal vessels remains intact. Additionally, there is no hyperemia or dilation of the disc vessels in cases of ODD, unlike in true papilledema. Ancillary testing that supports a diagnosis of ODD include the following: • B Scan (answer A): calcified drusen are highly reflective as shown in the image below • Autofluorescence (as shown above): drusen close enough to the optic nerve head surface demonstrate autofluorescence compared with the typically hypoautofluorescent optic nerve head in normal eyes or eyes with true papilledema. • Fluorescein angiography: true papilledema will display leakage at the optic nerve head while ODD typically do not leak • CT (rather than MRI, answer B): may be helpful in unclear cases as CT is superior to MRI for detection of calcium. Calcified drusen are hyperdense on CT. • OCT (of the nerve rather than macula, answer D): may show the discrete drusen with a hyper-reflective edge / border and a hypo-reflective core in some cases. While lumbar puncture with opening pressure (answer C) is important to obtain in cases of true papilledema (after neuroimaging), it has no role for the diagnosis of optic disc drusen. REFERENCE: Palmer E, Gale J, Crowston JG, Wells AP. Optic Nerve Head Drusen: An Update. Neuroophthalmology. 2018 Apr 25;42(6):367-384.

question: Which of the following is the most common type of visual field defect found in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)?

options.D: partial arcuate defects Topic: The Patient With Decreased Vision: Classification and Management

explanation: The Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial was the first multicenter, double- blind, randomized controlled clinical trial to evaluate the effect of oral acetazolamide on visual functioning in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). The study group consisted of individuals with mild IIH who were treated with low-sodium weight-reduction plus the maximally-tolerated dosage of acetazolamide (up to 4 grams/day). The control group consisted of individuals with mild IIH who were treated with low sodium weight-reduction plus a placebo. The primary outcome measure was the change in perimetric mean deviation (PMD) (using the Humphrey Field Analyzer) from baseline to month 6 in the most affected eye. This trial showed a statistically-significant improvement in PMD in those individuals taking oral acetazolamide compared to placebo at 6 months (i.e. 1.43 dB versus 0.71 dB; p=0.05). Other notable findings: • Vision-related quality of life (measured by the National Eye Institute VFQ-25) was significantly better in the acetazolamide group versus the study group (i.e. 8.33 versus 1.98; p=0.003). • Greater reduction in weight in the study group versus the control group (i.e. loss of 7.5 kg versus loss of -3.45 kg; p<0.001) The accompanying paper describing the baseline characteristics of these IIH study participants was notable for the following: • The most common symptom was headache (84%). Other common symptoms included transient visual obscurations (68%); pulse synchronous tinnitus (52%); back pain (53%); double vision (18%). • The most common type of visual field defects were: o Nerve fiber bundle (i.e. partial arcuate) defects with and without enlarged blind spot (~70-80%) o Enlarged blind spot alone (~12%) o Paracentral scotomas with and without an enlarged blind spot (~5-6%)

On exam, his best-corrected visual acuity is 20/80 OU. He shows generalized constriction of his visual fields on static perimetry. Which of the following statements regarding this patient's condition is most accurate?

options.A: This condition is generally progressive throughout one's lifetime
options.B: Young maternal age is a risk factor for this condition
options.C: Agenesis of corpus callosum is typically present

explanation: The disc photos and vignette are consistent with optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH). The optic discs in ONH are described as being smaller than normal; pale or gray in color; and often with a "double ring sign" (i.e. a ring of hypo- or hyperpigmentation surrounding the disc). Other notable facts regarding ONH: • Typically bilateral, but can be unilateral in 15-25% of cases. If the ONH is unilateral or asymmetrically bilateral, an afferent pupillary defect can be detected. • No proven gender predisposition. • Little correlation between the size of the optic discs and visual acuity. • Visual acuity can range from near normal to light perception. • ONH is considered a clinical diagnosis. Though some genes (e.g. HESX1) have been implicated in the development of ONH, there is not enough genotype/phenotype correlation for genetic testing to be useful in its diagnosis. • Some risk factors for its development: preterm birth, low birth weight, young maternal age, primiparity, prenatal exposure to certain toxins (e.g. smoking, alcohol), maternal diabetes, and maternal anemia. • ONH may occur as an isolated finding or in association with neurological/hormonal abnormalities. Approximately 27% of patients with ONH will have partial or complete absence of the septum pellucidum (i.e. septo-optic dysplasia aka "de Morsier's syndrome"). This condition's clinical findings include developmental delay, taste abnormalities, impaired smell, and spasticity. All the pituitary hormones may be adversely affected due to defects of the hypothalamus, infundibulum, or pituitary gland itself. Though there is no known treatment for ONH, a systemic evaluation is typically warranted in neonates diagnosed with ONH. This workup typically includes a MRI of the brain to look for structural abnormalities (e.g. hydrocephalus, corpus callosum hypoplasia) and an endocrinologic workup. REFERENCE: Kaur S, Jain S, Sodhi HB, Rastogi A, Kamlesh. Optic nerve hypoplasia. Oman J Ophthalmol. 2013 May;6(2):77-82. Maternal ingestion of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) has been associated most with which of the following congenital optic nerve abnormalities? A.morning glory syndrome (MGS) B.optic pit C.hypoplasia D.coloboma High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH) is associated with maternal ingestion of alcohol, quinine, phenytoin, and LSD. Other risk factors include: young maternal age, primiparity, pre-term labor, low maternal weight gain, and maternal weight loss during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. Segmental hypoplasia can occur in children born to mothers with type 1 diabetes. The disc in optic nerve hypoplasia is often small, pale or gray in color, and may exhibit the "double ring sign" (i.e. yellow-to-white ring around the disc). The outer ring is the normal junction between the sclera and the lamina cribrosa while the inner ring is the abnormal extension of the retina and RPE over the outer portion of the lamina cribrosa. Morning glory has an etiology that is poorly understood, but is not related to maternal LSD ingestion. Morning glory may be a part of other systemic abnormalities such as basal encephalocoele and midfacial malformations. Optic disc colobomas are often familial, bilateral, without sex predilection, and are not linked to maternal LSD ingestion. Colobomas can occur as part of other systemic conditions such as CHARGE (colobomas and cranial nerves, heart problems, atresia of the choanae, retardation of growth/development, genital and urinary abnormalities, ear and hearing abnormalities), Walker-Warburg syndrome, Aicardi syndrome, Goldenhar syndrome, and linear sebaceous nevus syndrome. An optic pit is a depression of the optic disc surface that is typically gray-white; located temporally; and associated with a mild visual field defect (e.g. paracentral or arcuate). An optic pit can lead to a serous macular detachment in 25-75% of cases. Optic pits are not associated with LSD ingestion. A 38-year-old man presents with a visual field defect that you interpret as bitemporal hemianopsia. His review of systems is significant for decreased libido and impotence preceding the visual changes. He embarrassingly also reveals to you the abnormality depicted in the photo above. Which of the following medical therapies would be most useful in treating this patient's underlying disease process? A.quetiapine B.droperidol C.cabertrigline D.bromocriptine High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The clinical vignette is alluding to a patient suffering from a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (i.e. prolactinoma or "lactotroph adenoma") that is compressing his optic chiasm causing a typical bitemoporal hemianopic visual field defect. The excess prolactin hormone levels causes characteristic changes in premenopausal women and in men (but not postmenopausal women). These are summarized here: Premenopausal women • infertility • irregular menstrual cycles (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea) • occasional galactorrhea Postmenopausal women • since these patients are already hypogonadal, they do not have the symptoms typical of hyperprolactinemia found in younger women. • instead, they may present with visual changes or headaches when/if the prolactinoma is large Men • decreased libido • impotence • gynecomastia (as seen in the photo) • occasional galactorrhea The majority of prolactinomas can be treated with dopamine agonists since dopamine is the natural neuroinhibitor of prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary. Examples of effective dopamine agonists include: bromocriptine, cabergoline, and pergolide. If medical treatment fails, then transsphenoidal surgery can be considered. Radiation treatment is sometimes used after surgical debulking, but not typically as a primary therapy for prolactinomas. (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons; http://commons.wikimedia.org)

explanation: This is an example of how intermittent angle closure glaucoma attacks can mimic migraine. The key here is that this patient has moderate hyperopia and her visual blurring is not typical of a migraine aura. Migrainous visual auras last 15-60 minutes and typically precede headaches. Angle closure attacks cause blurred vision that follows headache onset and may last much longer than 15-60 minutes. While this patient may have glaucomatous cupping with visual field deficits requiring the usual glaucoma work-up, it is important to make the diagnosis of intermittent angle closure first so she can undergo prompt peripheral laser iridotomy. Gonioscopy in the affected eye would be expected to show occludable angles and possible peripheral anterior synechiae. Standard slit lamp examination of the anterior chamber is NOT sufficient to evaluate this patient and CANNOT be used to rule out intermittent angle closure glaucoma. A 70-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of recurrent bouts of intermittent bilateral blurring of vision. The vision loss lasts 10 seconds to 10 minutes but always returns to normal. Associated with this vision loss is the sensation of vertigo and difficulty with balance which occur with the episodes but then resolve completely. The patient denies any history of headaches but does have a sister with migraine headaches. The patient also denies jaw claudication, diplopia, myalgias, fever, and unintentional weight loss. A referring primary care physician has already ordered carotid dopplers and an MRI which were normal. His exam is essentially unremarkable. What is the next best management step in this case? A.Order an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) B.Order a CT-angiogram (CTA) of the brain C.Start sumatriptan as necessary D.Order an electroencephalography (EEG) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation of vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency can arise from hypoperfusion of the vertebral, basilar, or posterior cerebral arteries. Symptoms result from brainstem, cerebellar, and/or occipital lobe dysfunction and include transient dimming/blacking out of both eyes, ataxia, vertigo, dysarthria, dysphagia, and hemiparesis / hemiplegia. An ESR and CRP could be ordered to evaluate for giant cell arteritis but this patient has no typical giant cell arteritis (GCA) symptoms and his visual blurring is highly atypical for GCA. GCA does not usually present with simultaneous bilateral transient vision loss and would likely have progressed to permanent vision loss after 6 months of symptoms. Usually, premonitory vision loss in GCA occurs within weeks of permanent vision loss. While this patient's account of vision loss could mimic migraine, it is highly atypical to develop new migraine auras at age 70. Also atypical, this patient has associated ataxia which is not expected from migraine. Isolated occipital lobe seizures detected by an EEG could cause bilateral transient vision loss but usually have positive visual phenomena (simple hallucinations, photopsias, etc) and would be highly unusual in this setting. Which patient would benefit the most from carotid endarterectomy (CEA)? (Note: the degree of stenosis was assessed by carotid ultrasound testing; if not mentioned assume no stenosis) A.A 70-year old male with asymptomatic 60% carotid stenosis bilaterally B.A 70-year old male with a history of recurrent amaurosis fugax OD and a complete right carotid occlusion C.A 70-year old male with a history of recurrent amaurosis fugax OD and 50% right carotid stenosis D.A 70-year old male with a history of recurrent amaurosis fugax OD and 80% right carotid stenosis High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy trial (NASCET) showed that patients with amaurosis fugax or hemispheric TIAs with 70-99% carotid stenosis benefitted from carotid endarterectomy to reduce the risk of future stroke. Studies have shown that endarterectomy for a completely-occluded carotid artery has a low success rate for re-establishing flow and a high mortality rate. The data for asymptomatic carotid stenosis is less reliable and is still debated. Most clinicians reserve CEA for symptomatic patients with stenosis. How long does temporary (often posture change related) vision loss associated with papilledema typically last? A.1-30 seconds B.5-15 minutes C.15-60 minutes D.1-2 days High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Papilledema often results in "transient visual obscurations" which are usually described as a binocular (assuming both eyes have papilledema) dimming / loss of vision lasting a matter of seconds. It is often precipitated by postural changes, eye movement, or Valsalva-like actions. While severe and/or chronic papilledema can cause permanent visual field defects, transient visual obscurations by definition do not cause long-term deficits. Answer choice B (5-15 minutes) represents the typical duration of vision loss in amaurosis fugax while answer choice C (15-60 minutes) represents the typical duration of vision loss in migraine related visual aura. Answer choice D (1-2 days) is an atypical duration for temporary vision loss due to organic disease. How long does temporary vision loss associated with migrainous aura typically last? A.1-30 seconds B.5-10 minutes C.10-60 minutes D.1-2 days High Yield: Yes Your Answer: B Correct Answer: C Explanation: Migraine headaches can be preceded by visual auras during which patients classically experience a scotoma with jagged shimmering edges that expand and migrate across the visual field in one or both eyes. While this is the classic description of a visual aura, there is a great deal of variability among the appearance of visual auras. Generally however, almost all visual auras last 10-60 minutes. This becomes important diagnostically when investigating temporary vision loss. Amaurosis fugax, for instance, generally lasts 1-10 minutes while transient visual obscurations associated with papilledema or optic nerve head drusen last for a matter of seconds only. A 70-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes presents with a 4-month history of a large central scotoma that appears in his right eye every time he is in a bright environment (walking outdoors on a sunny day, looking at a light indoors, etc). The scotoma generally lasts a matter of minutes once he exits the bright environment. He has had increasing intermittent periocular pain and ocular pain that improves with laying down and closing his eyes. He has no other ocular complaints. On exam his vision is 20/20 in both eyes with normal pupillary function and no afferent pupillary defect. The remainder of his exam was unremarkable aside from 3-4 mid-peripheral dot blot hemorrhages per quadrant in the right eye. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test in this setting? A.MRI of the brain B.CT of the orbits C.Traditional electroretinogram (ERG) D.Fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Light-induced amaurosis is a very characteristic finding of ocular ischemic syndrome (OIS). There are a number of reasonable diagnostic studies to order in evaluation of this patient including fluorescein angiography, carotid dopplers, CTA, or MRA. explanation: This is an example of how intermittent angle closure glaucoma attacks can mimic migraine. The key here is that this patient has moderate hyperopia and her visual blurring is not typical of a migraine aura. Migrainous visual auras last 15-60 minutes and typically precede headaches. Gonioscopy in the affected eye would be expected to show occludable angles and possible peripheral anterior synechiae. Standard slit lamp examination of the anterior chamber is NOT sufficient to evaluate this patient and CANNOT be used to rule out intermittent angle closure glaucoma. A 70-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of recurrent bouts of intermittent bilateral blurring of vision. The vision loss lasts 10 seconds to 10 minutes but always returns to normal. Associated with this vision loss is the sensation of vertigo and difficulty with balance which occur with the episodes but then resolve completely. The patient denies any history of headaches but does have a sister with migraine headaches. The patient also denies jaw claudication, diplopia, myalgias, fever, and unintentional weight loss. A referring primary care physician has already ordered carotid dopplers and an MRI which were normal. His exam is essentially unremarkable. What is the next best management step in this case? Vertebrobasilar insufficiency can arise from hypoperfusion of the vertebral, basilar, or posterior cerebral arteries. Symptoms result from brainstem, cerebellar, and/or occipital lobe dysfunction and include transient dimming/blacking out of both eyes, ataxia, vertigo, dysarthria, dysphagia, and hemiparesis / hemiplegia. Which patient would benefit the most from carotid endarterectomy (CEA)? (Note: the degree of stenosis was assessed by carotid ultrasound testing; if not mentioned assume no stenosis)

options.A: A 70-year old male with asymptomatic 60% carotid stenosis bilaterally
options.B: A 70-year old male with a history of recurrent amaurosis fugax OD and a complete right carotid occlusion
options.C: A 70-year old male with a history of recurrent amaurosis fugax OD and 50% right carotid stenosis
options.D: A 70-year old male with a history of recurrent amaurosis fugax OD and 80% right carotid stenosis

explanation: The North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy trial (NASCET) showed that patients with amaurosis fugax or hemispheric TIAs with 70-99% carotid stenosis benefitted from carotid endarterectomy to reduce the risk of future stroke. He has had increasing intermittent periocular pain and ocular pain that improves with laying down and closing his eyes. He has no other ocular complaints. On exam his vision is 20/20 in both eyes with normal pupillary function and no afferent pupillary defect. question: What additional testing would be helpful to definitely prove your working clinical diagnosis?
explanation: This is a classic presentation of adult-onset progressive external ophthalmoplegia typically referred to as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). This patient demonstrated moderate, symmetric motility deficits with slow saccades and bilateral upper eyelid ptosis on exam. This in combination with her asymptomatic presentation and 15 year history of bilateral ptosis is highly suggestive of CPEO. Orbicularlis oculi testing on the right showed marked weakness and this patient, in fact, had marked full facial weakness bilaterally (not shown in video). CPEO is a mitochondrial myopathy that predominately affects the extraocular muscles (EOMS) and the levator palpebrae superioris although a large percentage of these patients (in some series over 50%) have facial weakness and limb weakness. In the scenario of more widespread weakness, the literature may use the term “CPEO plus” syndrome. The literature today supports the notion that CPEO, CPEO plus, and Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS) (CPEO with pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction defects) all exist along a spectrum of disease. The earlier onset, more severe mitochondrial dysfunction manifests in a KSS phenotype while later onset disease may or may not be isolated to the extraocular muscles. The key teaching point of this question is recognizing the features of CPEO and distinguishing it from a mimicker like myasthenia gravis (MG) with ocular involvement. While myasthenia can on rare occasion present in a chronic relatively asymptomatic form and CPEO can very rarely seem to present acutely, the clinical presentation is vastly different in most. Most patients with MG causing ophthalmoplegia do have diplopia because of highly fatigable asymmetric EOM weakness. A CT chest would be indicated in a patient with confirmed MG to assess for a thymoma which is seen in around 10-20% of cases. A sfEMG is an excellent test for ocular MG without systemic involvement with a reported sensitivity around 90% but unfortunately testing is often abnormal in CPEO and sfEMG does not help in distinguishing these two diagnoses. Thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) is an excellent test to assess for thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) in that it is both sensitive and specific but this case does not have features of TAO such as eyelid retraction, proptosis, or ocular / periocular inflammatory signs. While a normal limb muscle biopsy does not completely rule out a CPEO diagnosis, a positive biopsy does definitely complete the diagnosis. Biopsies can be taken from alternative sites such as the levator palpebrae superioris and extraocular muscles but the risk of complication is higher in these areas.

question: The nystagmoid movement known as "ocular bobbing" localizes pathology to what structure in the central nervous system (CNS)?

options.D: The ciliary ganglion Category: Neuro-ophthalmology Topic: The Patient with Nystagmus Or Spontaneous Eye Movement Disorders

explanation: Ocular bobbing is an uncommon and unique nystagmus-like movement of the eyes that is usually indicative of brainstem disease (often localized to the pons). It consists of cycles of a conjugate fast downward movement of both eyes followed by a slow elevation of both eyes back to primary gaze. While this author is not sure of the origin of the term ocular bobbing, the movement is similar conceptually to the action of a bobber used when fishing. When the fish strikes a hook attached to a line and bobber, the bobber initially sinks rapidly but slowly returns to the surface as the fish tires. The most common causes include brainstem ischemia and stroke of the brainstem although severe metabolic encephalopathy without a structural abnormality of the brainstem can also cause ocular bobbing. There are a number of variants of ocular bobbing such as inverse bobbing (or ocular dipping), reverse ocular bobbing, and converse ocular bobbing. These variants describe alterations in the direction and speed of the fast and slow phases but the important aspect to all ocular bobbing type eye movement disorders is that they indicate brainstem dysfunction which is either structural or metabolic. Which of the following answers correctly describes the eye movement recordings characteristic of the infantile nystagmus waveform (also historically termed congenital nystagmus)? A.An exponential increase in fast phase velocity over time B.An exponential decrease in fast phase velocity over time C.An exponential increase in slow phase velocity over time D.An exponential decrease in slow phase velocity over time High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Despite its limited clinical relevance this seems to be a high yield fact regarding the congenital nystagmus waveform. First of all, the fast phase of any nystagmus will generally show a linear form with one speed. This makes sense when one considers the underlying mechanism of nystagmus which is that there is a pathologic slow deviation away from fixation followed by a quick recovery saccade. The recovery saccade is actually physiologic in the sense that it represents the mind attempting to re-establish normal fixation. Therefore the distinguishing waveform features between differing types of nystagmus include direction, frequency, symmetry between eyes, pendular versus jerk, and slow phase velocity / acceleration but not fast phase velocity / acceleration. The fact that the slow phase velocity in congenital nystagmus accelerates over time before initiation of the fast phase must simply be memorized. This is a distinguishing feature from the slow phase wave form of latent nystagmus which shows either a constant velocity or a decelerating velocity. Of note, the 2016-17 and prior Peds BCSCs describe the slow phase of latent nystagmus (aka fusional maldevelopment nystagmus) as decelerating only and infantile nystagmus (aka congenital nystagmus) as accelerating. The 2016-17 Neuro-op BCSC describes the slow phase of latent nystagmus as having a constant velocity. We were told by people in the know that this conflict will be resolved in future editions. The truth is that the slow phase of latent nystagmus either has a constant velocity or a decelerating velocity. A 40-year-old male presents with a 1 year history of intermittent diarrhea and nystagmoid eye movements. His visual acuity, pupils, visual fields, and IOP are normal. Motility exam is complicated by his abnormal ocular oscillations but appears full. He demonstrates bilateral rhythmic convergent oscillations of his eyes with bilateral rhythmic contraction of his jaw muscles. Attempts to distract the patient to see if the nystagmus is volitional fail suggesting this is not self-induced. What is the treatment of choice for this patient? A.Antibiotics B.IV steroids C.Reassurance D.gabapentin High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculomasticatory myorhythmia is a very rare eye / facial movement disorder seen only in Whipple disease with CNS involvement. Exactly as described in the question, it results in bilateral rhythmic convergent oscillations of the eyes along with rhythmic contraction of the muscles of mastication. While exceedingly rare it is highly testable because the finding is considered pathognomonic for CNS Whipple disease which is curable with appropriate antibiotic therapy. Other systemic (and more common) features of Whipple disease include chronic diarrhea from duodenal infestation with Tropheryma whippelii. Associated symptoms also include unexplained fevers, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy. The diagnosis is usually made on duodenal biopsy when PAS positive macrophage inclusions (representing the causative organisms) are seen. Outstanding OQ users have been kind enough to point out an excellent video of oculomasticatory myorhythmia available on the internet as filmed by an excellent neuro-ophthalmologist, Dr. Jack Selhorst. Please see the link(s): http://goo.gl/tHuf5q Link 2 Which of the following statements regarding oscillopsia is NOT true? A.Oscillopsia can be caused by true nystagmus as well as nystagmoid eye movements B.Oscillopsia can aide in distinguishing congenital nystagmus from acquired nystagmus C.Oscillopsia must be looked for carefully during the examination of all nystagmus patients D.Oscillopsia can differ in severity depending on gaze High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: Oscillopsia is the subjective movement of the environment in patients with quick eye movement disorders such as nystagmus and other nystagmoid type eye movements that don't meet the strict definition of nystagmus. Oscillopsia is a subjective complaint so therefore it can not be seen on examination (similar to how an examiner can not see double vision on exam). It is helpful in the sense that patients with acquired nystagmus tend to have oscillopsia while those with congenital nystagmus tend to adapt without oscillopsia. In patients with oscillopsia, the severity of the symptoms correlates to the severity of the nystagmus. Patients with down beat nystagmus, for instance, will often note that the oscillopsia is worse in lateral gaze. On examination those same patients will demonstrate a more prominent nystagmus in lateral gaze. A 60-year-old patient with diabetes and hypertension suffers a large right hemisphere stroke of the middle cerebral artery affecting the right frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. Which one of the following ocular / visual sequelae of his stroke would be expected to improve dramatically within a week? A.Right gaze deviation B.Left homonymous hemianopia C.Smooth pursuit to the right D.None High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Hemispheric strokes can affect the afferent and efferent function of the eyes in multiple ways. The general rule of stroke is that infarcted neurons do not recover function in adults. The exception to this rule is that patients with a gaze deviation towards the side of the infarct due to dysfunction of the frontal eye field (Brodmann area 8) recover quickly. Remember the frontal eye field exerts supranuclear control over lateral gaze towards the opposite side so an infarct of the right frontal lobe will result in a temporary right gaze deviation. A seizure, however, in the region of the frontal eye field will cause an episodic deviation towards the contralateral side. The hypothesis proposed to explain the quick recovery from supranuclear gaze deviations caused by hemispheric strokes (usually a matter of days) is that the brain compensates by using other viable neurons to serve the same function. Another hypothesis is that the brain simply "recalibrates" ocular alignment shortly after infarction of the frontal eye field. Infarction of axons passing through the optic radiations (either the temporal, parietal or occipital lobe) from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex would result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Such a visual field defect may improve slightly over time as the patient learns to adapt to his/her deficit but the deficit would not be expected to improve dramatically or quickly. The circuitry for horizontal smooth pursuit is complex. As one of many structures important for smooth pursuit, the parietal lobe permits smooth pursuit of objects tracking towards the same side. A right parietal lobe stroke would be expected to permanently impair smooth pursuit towards the right. Which of the following would NOT be a characteristic of latent nystagmus (LN)? A.Conjugate bilateral jerk nystagmus B.Fast phase beating away from the occluded eye C.Highly associated with exotropia D.Caused by disruption of normal development of binocular fusion High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Latent nystagmus (LN) is a form of nystagmus that develops early in life and most likely occurs from early disruption of binocular vision. For that reason it is very common in children with infantile strabismus, specifically esotropia. While it could occur in association with exotropia, the vast majority of LN is associated with esotropia. LN is generally asymptomatic for most patients (unless it becomes manifest) but can result in poor visual acuity results on monocular vision testing. The nystagmus is a BILATERAL jerk nystagmus that generally only manifests upon occlusion of one eye. The fast phase of the nystagmus beats towards the viewing eye. Surgeries for nystagmus involving detachment and reattachment of the extraocular muscles (such as the Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure) should be avoided in which of the following patients? A.Patients with periodic alternating nystagmus B.Patients with a null point in up gaze or down gaze C.Patients with an eccentric null point and strabismus D.Patients with nystagmus blockage syndrome High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) is a form of bilateral, horizontal jerk nystagmus that alternates fast phase directions following a reliable time cycle (usually 2-4 minutes). The cycle begins with a static phase devoid of nystagmus and is followed by crescendo then decrescendo jerk nystagmus to one side. A return to the static phase occurs after which there is a crescendo / decrescendo jerk nystagmus to the opposite side. The cycle then terminates with another static phase. PAN may be congenital or acquired. Because of the reliability of the short cycle and the importance of diagnosis, all patients with horizontal jerk nystagmus should be observed for a minimum of 2 minutes to ensure that the diagnosis of PAN is not missed. One of the greatest concerns in missing the diagnosis of PAN is that the null point in patients with PAN can alternate depending on the direction of the jerk nystagmus. For this reason, Kestenbaum surgery or Kestenbaum variants used to shift the null point to primary gaze should be avoided in these patients unless it is clear that the patient always maintains the same null point throughout the PAN cycle. Patients with null points on up gaze or down gaze are still good candidates for surgery but the vertical acting muscles are adjusted rather than the horizontal muscles as in the Kestenbaum- Anderson procedure. Nystagmus blockage syndrome is a condition in which convergence is used as a null point to block nystagmus. Symptoms can be ameliorated in these cases by recessing the medial recti muscles. Finally, strabismus repair can be combined with nystagmus surgery without complications. What two nystagmoid (or nystagmus-like) eye movements are considered saccadic intrusions and demonstrate nystagmoid eye movements without an intersaccadic interval? A.Ocular flutter and opsoclonus B.Square wave jerks and ocular flutter C.Square wave jerks and opsoclonus D.Superior oblique myokymia and square wave jerks High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. In pendular nystagmus, the fast phase and slow phase have the same velocity but it is still considered a true nystagmus. Ocular flutter, opsoclonus, square wave jerks, and superior oblique myokymia are all nystagmoid movements because they do not exhibit the biphasic or rhythmic characteristics of nystagmus. Square-wave jerks (SWJs) are a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or intersaccadic interval) and then a quick return to fixation. Superior oblique myokymia is a high frequency monocular oscillation caused by spontaneous firing of the superior oblique muscle. Superior oblique myokymia is generally episodic and short lived with long pauses between attacks. Opsoclonus is also known as saccadomania and is a dramatic bilateral eye movement disorder marked by involuntary multidirectional saccades without an intersaccadic "quiet" interval. Ocular flutter is similar to opsoclonus except it consists of repetitive purely horizontal saccades without an intersaccadic interval of rest which leads to the appearance of fluttering. hich of the following types of nystagmus is commonly associated with a visual field defect? A.Downbeat nystagmus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Most types of nystagmus are not localizable to dysfunction of one particular structure in the brain. Many forms of nystagmus, however, are associated with pathology of the lower brainstem and cerebellum including periodic alternating nystagmus, upbeat nystagmus, and downbeat nystagmus. See-saw nystagmus is a disconjugate nystagmus marked by one eye that elevated and intorts while another eye depresses and extorts. See saw nystagmus is exceptional in that it usually localizes to pathology in the diencephalon / parasellar region. For this reason it is the one of the few nystagmus forms associated with a visual field defect (bitemporal hemianopia). Which of the following types of nystagmus is NOT usually caused by lower brainstem or cerebellar pathology? A.See-saw nystagmus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.Downbeat nystagmus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Nystagmus is a confusing topic and poorly understood in general. Most types of nystagmus are not localizable to dysfunction of one particular structure in the brain. Many forms of nystagmus, however, are associated with pathology of the brainstem and cerebellum including periodic alternating nystagmus, upbeat nystagmus, and downbeat nystagmus. See-saw nystagmus is a disconjugate nystagmus marked by one eye that elevated and intorts while another eye depresses and extorts. See saw nystagmus is exceptional in that it usually localizes to pathology in the diencephalon / parasellar region. For this reason it is the one of the few nystagmus forms associated with a visual field defect (bitemporal hemianopia). The name see-saw is an excellent mnemonic actually. Imagine 2 large eye balls on a see- saw that is constantly pivoting (see diagram below and imagine the fulcrum is the patient’s nose). The eyeball on the high-side is going to roll down (incyclotort) while the low-side eyeball is also going to roll down (excyclotort). When the see saw pivots the other way each eye will cyclotort the other way.

question: Surgeries for nystagmus involving detachment and reattachment of the extraocular muscles (such as the Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure) should be avoided in which of the following patients?

options.B: Patients with a null point in up gaze or down gaze
options.C: Patients with an eccentric null point and strabismus

explanation: Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) is a form of bilateral, horizontal jerk nystagmus that alternates fast phase directions following a reliable time cycle (usually 2-4 minutes). The cycle begins with a static phase devoid of nystagmus and is followed by crescendo then decrescendo jerk nystagmus to one side. A return to the static phase occurs after which there is a crescendo / decrescendo jerk nystagmus to the opposite side. The cycle then terminates with another static phase. PAN may be congenital or acquired. Because of the reliability of the short cycle and the importance of diagnosis, all patients with horizontal jerk nystagmus should be observed for a minimum of 2 minutes to ensure that the diagnosis of PAN is not missed. One of the greatest concerns in missing the diagnosis of PAN is that the null point in patients with PAN can alternate depending on the direction of the jerk nystagmus. For this reason, Kestenbaum surgery or Kestenbaum variants used to shift the null point to primary gaze should be avoided in these patients unless it is clear that the patient always maintains the same null point throughout the PAN cycle. Patients with null points on up gaze or down gaze are still good candidates for surgery but the vertical acting muscles are adjusted rather than the horizontal muscles as in the Kestenbaum- Anderson procedure. Nystagmus blockage syndrome is a condition in which convergence is used as a null point to block nystagmus. Symptoms can be ameliorated in these cases by recessing the medial recti muscles. Finally, strabismus repair can be combined with nystagmus surgery without complications. question: Pathology of what structure results in rebound nystagmus?
explanation: Rebound nystagmus occurs following prolonged eccentric gaze. The neural integrator (comprised of different brainstem structures depending on whether maintaining vertical or horizontal gaze) allows the eyes to maintain eccentric gaze by regulating the innervational tone necessary to overcome elastic forces in the orbit pushing the eye back towards primary gaze. In people with cerebellar disease, there is poor coordination of the neural integrator input leading to gaze-evoked nystagmus. Gaze-evoked nystagmus is caused by an inability to overcome the elastic forces of the orbit on far horizontal or vertical gaze. On attempted eccentric gaze, there is a slow drift back towards primary gaze followed by a fast recovery saccade in the direction of the eccentric gaze to attempt to maintain the eyes' far eccentric position. Rebound nystagmus is different than gaze-evoked nystagmus and is best explained by example. After prolonged eccentric gaze to the right with right beating gaze-evoked nystagmus, if the eyes are returned to primary gaze there may be residual tone pushing the eye towards the right. Rebound nystagmus will be perceived by the observer as a slow rightward deviation of the eyes in primary gaze followed by a corrective left beating fast phase. The neural circuitry gets confusing quickly but the take home message is that cerebellar disease causes both gaze- evoked nystagmus AND rebound nystagmus. Rebound nystagmus occurs for a matter of seconds after the eyes are brought to primary gaze following prolonged eccentric gaze and is marked by a fast phase nystagmus opposite to the previous gaze direction. Which of the following types of nystagmus is associated with hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI? A.Periodic alternating nystagmus B.Oculopalatal myoclonus related pendular nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: B Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is classically vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. One OQ user brought to our attention this excellent website showing the characteristic changes of inferior olivary hypertrophy: http://radiopaedia.org/articles/hypertrophic-olivary-degeneration What is the correct description of latent nystagmus (LN)? A.Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye B.Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye C.Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye. D.Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye. High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Latent nystagmus (LN) is a form of nystagmus that develops early in life and mostly likely occurs from early disruption of binocular vision. For that reason it is very common in children with infantile strabismus. LN is generally asymptomatic for most patients (unless it becomes manifest) but can result in poor visual acuity results on monocular vision testing. The nystagmus is a BILATERAL jerk nystagmus that generally only manifests upon occlusion of one eye. The fast phase of the nystagmus beats towards the viewing eye. Some may think of LN as monocular because it is observed clinically when one eye is covered but the occluded eye also has nystagmus. When testing vision in children with LN, optical blurring of one eye is preferable to occlusion because it does not incite as much nystagmus in the viewing eye thus allowing a more accurate acuity measurement. A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Which of the following is actually a misnomer in that it does not meet the definition of a true nystagmus? A.Periodic alternating nystagmus B.Congenital nystagmus C.Convergence-retraction nystagmus D.Downbeat nystagmus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. In pendular nystagmus, the fast phase and slow phase have the same velocity but it is still considered a true nystagmus. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is one component of the dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka Parinaud's syndrome) and is marked by abnormal co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted up-gaze. This abnormal eye movement is not rhythmic, does not have a fast or slow phase, and doesn't involve an abnormal drift from fixation. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with vascular compression induced neuropathy by an aberrant, ectatic, or dilated intracranial artery compressing on a cranial nerve? A.Benign essential blepharospasm B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Trigeminal neuralgia D.Hemifacial spasm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: As the resolution and availability of neuro-imaging improves, more neurological diseases have been found to arise from vascular compression of intracranial nerves. Superior oblique myokymia is a disease marked by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. In at least some cases, MRI has shown vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Trigeminal neuralgia is a pain disorder marked by severe unilateral paroxysmal shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution that is usually transient (lasting seconds or less). It can have multiple etiologies but vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is a well established cause; some patients with severe trigeminal neuralgia are treated surgically by microvascular decompression with placement of a sponge between the superior cerebellar artery and the trigeminal nerve. Hemifacial spasm is generally a unilateral disorder marked by abnormal spasms of the facial muscles supplied by CN7. Hemifacial spasm has numerous causes including stroke, demyelination, tumors, AVMs, and idiopathic disease. MRI studies now show that many cases previously thought to be idiopathic, however, are actually caused by vascular compression of the facial nerve root by the distal branches of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, or vertebral artery. In severe cases refractory to medication and/or botox, microvascular decompression surgery (similar to that performed for trigeminal neuralgia) can be performed and has been successful in the past. Benign essential blepharospasm is generally a bilateral disease with pronounced episodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles. There is some evidence that benign essential blepharospasm is related to underlying basal ganglia dysfunction but many patients also have a functional or stress related component. Symptoms may be exacerbated by corneal surface disease such as dry eye. The MRI in benign essential blepharospasm patients is virtually always normal and does not suggest a vascular compressive etiology. Which of the following history and exam features are NOT helpful in distinguishing voluntary (or self-induced) nystagmoid movements from other involuntary forms of nystagmus and nystagmoid movements? A.Associated facial grimacing and eyelid flutter B.Disappearance of oscillations with distraction C.Associated convergence movements D.Lack of oscillopsia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The most common functional neuro-ophthalmic complaints probably involve vision loss but functional or voluntary nystagmoid movements can present to your clinic as well. The diagnosis of volitional nystagmoid movements can usually be made easily in the clinic by looking for associated facial grimacing or eyelid flutter. Distracting the patient by having them perform tasks often breaks a cycle of oscillations. Usually the eye movements are low amplitude and associated with convergence movements so it is nearly impossible for the patient to maintain the performance when testing far lateral gaze on motility exam. It requires a great deal of effort to sustain volitional oscillations for more than a few seconds so it is helpful when attacks are noted to last only a few seconds. Oscillopsia is the sensation that the visual field is moving and is much more commonly described by patients with acquired nystagmus and nystagmoid eye movements. Its presence or absence on history, however, is not helpful in diagnosing voluntary nystagmoid eye movements. 16-month-old boy presents to your eye clinic because his parents noted his right eye "shaking" for the past month. Your exam shows fix, follow, intermittent maintain "FF(M)" vision OD and fix, follow, and maintain "FFM" vision OS. The pupil exam shows a trace APD OD. Motility is full and alignment is orthophoric based on alternate cover testing. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OD and -1.00 OS. External exam reveals a fine shimmering vertical nystagmus in the right eye with no nystagmus seen in the left eye. No head bobbing or torticollis is seen. Slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable. What is the next most appropriate step in the care of this patient? A.Prescribe glasses and follow-up in 3 months for re-evaluation B.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation C.Observe with repeat examination in 3 months D.Patch the left eye 6 hours daily and return in 3 month High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Monocular nystagmus in a child should immediately raise concerns for an optic nerve glioma. A monocular, small amplitude vertical nystagmus has been referred to as the Heimann- Bielschowsky phenomenon and may occur in association with any cause of decreased vision including amblyopia. This patient does have anisometropia which could cause amblyopia and account for his mild decrease in vision OD. The APD in the right eye is highly concerning for organic pathology, however. Severe amblyopia can result in a mild APD but in this situation organic pathology (such as a glioma) of the optic nerve, chiasm, or tract must be excluded. Spasmus nutans, a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding, can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans. The parents of a 4-year-old boy with torticollis and vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye since 1 year of age come to your clinic for a second opinion. The patient was diagnosed with spasmus nutans by another provider at presentation 3 years ago after a reportedly normal MRI. By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. His visual field is full to confrontation with finger count techniques, motility normal, and alignment orthophoric by alternate cover testing. The patient was uncooperative for pupillary testing so it was difficult to assess for an APD although his pupils reacted to light bilaterally. External exam confirms a monocular vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye and torticollis with a right head tilt. His penlight anterior segment exam is grossly normal and dilated fundus exam reveals trace pallor of the right optic nerve. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in both eyes. What is the next best step in the care of this patient? A.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation B.Reassure the parents and have the patient follow-up in one year C.Prescribe glasses and have the patient follow-up in one year D.Initiate patching for 6 hours daily in the left eye. High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Spasmus nutans is a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding. The nystagmus is frequently referred to as "shimmering" due to its high frequency low amplitude nature. The nystagmus is usually horizontal and bilateral although it may be unilateral, vertical, or rotary. It usually presents within the first 2 years of life and then resolves within 1-2 years. Spasmus nutans can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans to rule out an anterior optic pathway glioma. This patient appropriately underwent an MRI at the time of diagnosis which was normal. After 3 years, however, his nystagmus and torticollis have not resolved which is alarming. Also, this patient has unexplained decreased visual acuity in the right eye along with optic nerve pallor increasing concern for optic nerve pathology such as an anterior optic pathway glioma. When spasmus nutans does not recover as expected or is associated with additional neurological deficits then repeat neuro-imaging is warranted. Which of the following is NOT a recognized cause of downbeat nystagmus? A.Arnold-Chiari type I malformation B.Demyelination the cerebellum and/or medulla C.Migraine D.Magnesium deficiency High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: C Explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (DBN) is the result of abnormal drift of the eyes upward followed by a corrective downward fast saccade. Most pathology causing DBN localizes to the cervicomedullary junction (CVMJ) or cerebellum. MRI of the brain is warranted for evaluation of DBN because structural lesions of the CVMJ or cerebellum including Arnold-Chiari malformation, mass lesions (meningioma or hemangioma), and syrinx are causes of DBN and may be amenable to surgical intervention. Other causes include drug-induced cerebellar dysfunction (ETOH, lithium, anticonvulsants), stroke, demyelination, and poor nutrition (magnesium deficiency, Wernicke's encephalopathy). Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) that are usually associated with stiff person syndrome can also cause DBN. Paraneoplastic anti-neuronal antibodies have also been associated with DBN so acute onset DBN may warrant a paraneoplastic panel and/or imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to look for the primary malignancy. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of congenital nystagmus? A.Presence of a null point B.Predominantly a conjugate, vertical nystagmus C.Manifests with either pendular or jerk nystagmus D.Intensifies with viewing of objects at distance High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital nystagmus is a highly tested topic. The features of congenital nystagmus can be remembered by a handy mnemonic CONGENITAL. What is the standard "cycle" time required for periodic alternating nystagmus to pass from the static (nystagmus free) phase through two nystagmus phases in different directions and back to a static phase?
