A 17-year-old female presents with a complaint of intermittent blurred vision for the past 2 years and inability to “focus.” Friends and family have noticed her eyes shaking at times. She has a past medical history of anxiety for which she takes Cymbalta and no past ocular history. Her exam is notable for the eye movement abnormality noted in the video below. She already underwent an MRI of the brain with and without IV contrast ordered by her primary care physician 2 months and this was unremarkable. Note that the patient was pharmacologically dilated at the time of the video. (there is a missing video) What is the next best step in the management of this patient? The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high-frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (though not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and / or convergence movements. The video clearly shows short bursts of low amplitude, high frequency “shimmering” horizontal nystagmus. At one point the patient actually stops to forcefully squeeze her eyelids- a sign that she is exerting considerable effort to produce the effect. Notice her eyelids are virtually always fluttering at the same time as her horizontal nystagmus. While not shown on the video, she did not exhibit the nystagmus on smooth pursuit motility testing which is characteristic of volitional nystagmus. If the patient had ocular flutter with a clean MRI brain, paraneoplastic causes could be considered and a work-up would include body imaging for malignancy, paraneoplastic antibodies, a careful female examination to assess for breast or ovarian cancer, and consideration of dedicated breast imaging if body imaging negative. This patient’s young age and 2 year history of symptoms would be unusual for paraneoplastic disease. MRI of the orbits would not provide any additional insight in this case.

question: Which of the following types of nystagmus is associated with hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI?
explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is classically vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. A.Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye B.Under monocular conditions, bilateral jerk nystagmus occurs with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye C.Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the viewing eye. D.Under monocular conditions, there is unilateral jerk nystagmus of the viewing eye with the fast phase beating towards the occluded eye. High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Latent nystagmus (LN) is a form of nystagmus that develops early in life and mostly likely occurs from early disruption of binocular vision. For that reason it is very common in children with infantile strabismus. LN is generally asymptomatic for most patients (unless it becomes manifest) but can result in poor visual acuity results on monocular vision testing. The nystagmus is a BILATERAL jerk nystagmus that generally only manifests upon occlusion of one eye. The fast phase of the nystagmus beats towards the viewing eye. Some may think of LN as monocular because it is observed clinically when one eye is covered but the occluded eye also has nystagmus. When testing vision in children with LN, optical blurring of one eye is preferable to occlusion because it does not incite as much nystagmus in the viewing eye thus allowing a more accurate acuity measurement. Which of the following is actually a misnomer in that it does not meet the definition of a true nystagmus? A.Periodic alternating nystagmus B.Congenital nystagmus C.Convergence-retraction nystagmus D.Downbeat nystagmus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with vascular compression induced neuropathy by an aberrant, ectatic, or dilated intracranial artery compressing on a cranial nerve? A.Benign essential blepharospasm B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Trigeminal neuralgia D.Hemifacial spasm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: As the resolution and availability of neuro-imaging improves, more neurological diseases have been found to arise from vascular compression of intracranial nerves. Superior oblique myokymia is a disease marked by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. In at least some cases, MRI has shown vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Trigeminal neuralgia is a pain disorder marked by severe unilateral paroxysmal shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution that is usually transient (lasting seconds or less). It can have multiple etiologies but vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is a well established cause; some patients with severe trigeminal neuralgia are treated surgically by microvascular decompression with placement of a sponge between the superior cerebellar artery and the trigeminal nerve. Hemifacial spasm is generally a unilateral disorder marked by abnormal spasms of the facial muscles supplied by CN7. Hemifacial spasm has numerous causes including stroke, demyelination, tumors, AVMs, and idiopathic disease. MRI studies now show that many cases previously thought to be idiopathic, however, are actually caused by vascular compression of the facial nerve root by the distal branches of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, or vertebral artery. In severe cases refractory to medication and/or botox, microvascular decompression surgery (similar to that performed for trigeminal neuralgia) can be performed and has been successful in the past. Benign essential blepharospasm is generally a bilateral disease with pronounced episodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles. There is some evidence that benign essential blepharospasm is related to underlying basal ganglia dysfunction but many patients also have a functional or stress related component. Symptoms may be exacerbated by corneal surface disease such as dry eye. The MRI in benign essential blepharospasm patients is virtually always normal and does not suggest a vascular compressive etiology. Which of the following history and exam features are NOT helpful in distinguishing voluntary (or self-induced) nystagmoid movements from other involuntary forms of nystagmus and nystagmoid movements? The diagnosis of volitional nystagmoid movements can usually be made easily in the clinic by looking for associated facial grimacing or eyelid flutter. Distracting the patient by having them perform tasks often breaks a cycle of oscillations. Usually the eye movements are low amplitude and associated with convergence movements so it is nearly impossible for the patient to maintain the performance when testing far lateral gaze on motility exam. It requires a great deal of effort to sustain volitional oscillations for more than a few seconds so it is helpful when attacks are noted to last only a few seconds. Its presence or absence on history, however, is not helpful in diagnosing voluntary nystagmoid eye movements. 16-month-old boy presents to your eye clinic because his parents noted his right eye "shaking" for the past month. Your exam shows fix, follow, intermittent maintain "FF(M)" vision OD and fix, follow, and maintain "FFM" vision OS. The pupil exam shows a trace APD OD. Motility is full and alignment is orthophoric based on alternate cover testing. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OD and -1.00 OS. External exam reveals a fine shimmering vertical nystagmus in the right eye with no nystagmus seen in the left eye. No head bobbing or torticollis is seen. Slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable. What is the next most appropriate step in the care of this patient? A monocular, small amplitude vertical nystagmus has been referred to as the Heimann- Bielschowsky phenomenon and may occur in association with any cause of decreased vision including amblyopia. This patient does have anisometropia which could cause amblyopia and account for his mild decrease in vision OD. The APD in the right eye is highly concerning for organic pathology, however. Severe amblyopia can result in a mild APD but in this situation organic pathology (such as a glioma) of the optic nerve, chiasm, or tract must be excluded. Spasmus nutans, a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding, can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans. The parents of a 4-year-old boy with torticollis and vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye since 1 year of age come to your clinic for a second opinion. The patient was diagnosed with spasmus nutans by another provider at presentation 3 years ago after a reportedly normal MRI. By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. His visual field is full to confrontation with finger count techniques, motility normal, and alignment orthophoric by alternate cover testing. The patient was uncooperative for pupillary testing so it was difficult to assess for an APD although his pupils reacted to light bilaterally. External exam confirms a monocular vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye and torticollis with a right head tilt. His penlight anterior segment exam is grossly normal and dilated fundus exam reveals trace pallor of the right optic nerve. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in both eyes. What is the next best step in the care of this patient? A.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation B.Reassure the parents and have the patient follow-up in one year C.Prescribe glasses and have the patient follow-up in one year D.Initiate patching for 6 hours daily in the left eye. High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Spasmus nutans is a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding. The nystagmus is frequently referred to as "shimmering" due to its high frequency low amplitude nature. This patient appropriately underwent an MRI at the time of diagnosis which was normal. After 3 years, however, his nystagmus and torticollis have not resolved which is alarming. Also, this patient has unexplained decreased visual acuity in the right eye along with optic nerve pallor increasing concern for optic nerve pathology such as an anterior optic pathway glioma. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with vascular compression induced neuropathy by an aberrant, ectatic, or dilated intracranial artery compressing on a cranial nerve? By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. Which of the following is NOT a recognized cause of downbeat nystagmus? A.Arnold-Chiari type I malformation B.Demyelination the cerebellum and/or medulla C.Migraine D.Magnesium deficiency High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: C Explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (DBN) is the result of abnormal drift of the eyes upward followed by a corrective downward fast saccade. Most pathology causing DBN localizes to the cervicomedullary junction (CVMJ) or cerebellum. MRI of the brain is warranted for evaluation of DBN because structural lesions of the CVMJ or cerebellum including Arnold-Chiari malformation, mass lesions (meningioma or hemangioma), and syrinx are causes of DBN and may be amenable to surgical intervention. Other causes include drug-induced cerebellar dysfunction (ETOH, lithium, anticonvulsants), stroke, demyelination, and poor nutrition (magnesium deficiency, Wernicke's encephalopathy). Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) that are usually associated with stiff person syndrome can also cause DBN. Paraneoplastic anti-neuronal antibodies have also been associated with DBN so acute onset DBN may warrant a paraneoplastic panel and/or imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to look for the primary malignancy. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of congenital nystagmus? A.Presence of a null point B.Predominantly a conjugate, vertical nystagmus C.Manifests with either pendular or jerk nystagmus D.Intensifies with viewing of objects at distance High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital nystagmus is a highly tested topic. The features of congenital nystagmus can be remembered by a handy mnemonic CONGENITAL. Convergence and eye closure dampen the nystagmus; Oscillopsia is usually absent; Null zone is present; Gaze position does not change the direction of nystagmus; Equal amplitude and frequency of nystagmus in each eye; Near acuity is good because convergence dampens the nystagmus; Inversion of optokinetic nystagmus occurs; Turning of head or abnormal head posture to allow eyes to enter a null zone leads to better visual acuity; Absent nystagmus during sleep; Latent nystagmus occurs. A.Nomenclature based on direction of the slow phase B.Consisting of a fast and slow phase C.Characterized by amplitude and velocity D.Rhythmic High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Nystagmus is a disorder marked by excessive eye movements that are rhythmic. What is the standard "cycle" time required for periodic alternating nystagmus to pass from the static (nystagmus free) phase through two nystagmus phases in different directions and back to a static phase? A.5-10 seconds B.15-45 seconds C.1-2 minutes D.2-4 minutes High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) is a form of bilateral, horizontal jerk nystagmus that alternates fast phase directions following a reliable time cycle (usually 2-4 minutes). A 17-year-old female presents with a complaint of intermittent blurred vision for the past 2 years and inability to “focus.” Friends and family have noticed her eyes shaking at times. She has a past medical history of anxiety for which she takes Cymbalta and no past ocular history. Her exam is notable for the eye movement abnormality noted in the video below. She already underwent an MRI of the brain with and without IV contrast ordered by her primary care physician 2 months and this was unremarkable. Note that the patient was pharmacologically dilated at the time of the video. (there is a missing video) What is the next best step in the management of this patient? A.Reassurance with no further work-up B.Referral for breast and pelvic examination by an OBGYN C.MRI of the orbits with and without IV contrast D.Order serum paraneoplastic antibody panel ‘ High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: This video depicts a textbook example of volitional nystagmus or voluntary nystagmus (VN). VN can be performed by a surprisingly high number of individuals (up to 8% of the general population in one study). While for most it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high-frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (though not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and / or convergence movements. The video clearly shows short bursts of low amplitude, high frequency “shimmering” horizontal nystagmus. At one point the patient actually stops to forcefully squeeze her eyelids- a sign that she is exerting considerable effort to produce the effect. Notice her eyelids are virtually always fluttering at the same time as her horizontal nystagmus. While not shown on the video, she did not exhibit the nystagmus on smooth pursuit motility testing which is characteristic of volitional nystagmus. The main differential diagnoses in this case would be acquired horizontal pendular nystagmus and ocular flutter neither of which would be so dramatically intermittent nor associated with eyelid fluttering. In the case of acquired ocular flutter, the differential diagnosis is essentially identical to opsoclonus and would include post-infectious autoimmune cases, paraneoplastic, and cerebellar / brainstem disease that would be seen on MRI (e.g. multiple sclerosis or neoplasm or inflammation). If the patient had ocular flutter with a clean MRI brain, paraneoplastic causes could be considered and a work-up would include body imaging for malignancy, paraneoplastic antibodies, a careful female examination to assess for breast or ovarian cancer, and consideration of dedicated breast imaging if body imaging negative. This patient’s young age and 2 year history of symptoms would be unusual for paraneoplastic disease. MRI of the orbits would not provide any additional insight in this case.

question: Some may think of LN as monocular because it is observed clinically when one eye is covered but the occluded eye also has nystagmus. When testing vision in children with LN, optical blurring of one eye is preferable to occlusion because it does not incite as much nystagmus in the viewing eye thus allowing a more accurate acuity measurement. Which of the following types of nystagmus is caused by a lesion of the central tegmental tract?
explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. question: Which of the following is actually a misnomer in that it does not meet the definition of a true nystagmus?
explanation: Nystagmus is an abnormal rhythmic oscillation of the eyes with a slow phase in which the eye drifts from its intended target and a fast phase marked by a quick corrective saccade back to the target. In pendular nystagmus, the fast phase and slow phase have the same velocity but it is still considered a true nystagmus. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is one component of the dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka Parinaud's syndrome) and is marked by abnormal co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted up-gaze. This abnormal eye movement is not rhythmic, does not have a fast or slow phase, and doesn't involve an abnormal drift from fixation. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with vascular compression induced neuropathy by an aberrant, ectatic, or dilated intracranial artery compressing on a cranial nerve? A.Benign essential blepharospasm B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Trigeminal neuralgia D.Hemifacial spasm High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: As the resolution and availability of neuro-imaging improves, more neurological diseases have been found to arise from vascular compression of intracranial nerves. Superior oblique myokymia is a disease marked by episodic paroxysmal contraction of the superior oblique on one side causing a "jumping" of vision in one eye and binocular diplopia. In at least some cases, MRI has shown vascular compression of the 4th nerve on the affected side. Trigeminal neuralgia is a pain disorder marked by severe unilateral paroxysmal shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution that is usually transient (lasting seconds or less). It can have multiple etiologies but vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is a well established cause; some patients with severe trigeminal neuralgia are treated surgically by microvascular decompression with placement of a sponge between the superior cerebellar artery and the trigeminal nerve. Hemifacial spasm is generally a unilateral disorder marked by abnormal spasms of the facial muscles supplied by CN7. Hemifacial spasm has numerous causes including stroke, demyelination, tumors, AVMs, and idiopathic disease. MRI studies now show that many cases previously thought to be idiopathic, however, are actually caused by vascular compression of the facial nerve root by the distal branches of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, or vertebral artery. In severe cases refractory to medication and/or botox, microvascular decompression surgery (similar to that performed for trigeminal neuralgia) can be performed and has been successful in the past. Benign essential blepharospasm is generally a bilateral disease with pronounced episodic contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles. There is some evidence that benign essential blepharospasm is related to underlying basal ganglia dysfunction but many patients also have a functional or stress related component. Symptoms may be exacerbated by corneal surface disease such as dry eye. The MRI in benign essential blepharospasm patients is virtually always normal and does not suggest a vascular compressive etiology. Which of the following history and exam features are NOT helpful in distinguishing voluntary (or self-induced) nystagmoid movements from other involuntary forms of nystagmus and nystagmoid movements? A.Associated facial grimacing and eyelid flutter B.Disappearance of oscillations with distraction C.Associated convergence movements D.Lack of oscillopsia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The most common functional neuro-ophthalmic complaints probably involve vision loss but functional or voluntary nystagmoid movements can present to your clinic as well. The diagnosis of volitional nystagmoid movements can usually be made easily in the clinic by looking for associated facial grimacing or eyelid flutter. Distracting the patient by having them perform tasks often breaks a cycle of oscillations. Usually the eye movements are low amplitude and associated with convergence movements so it is nearly impossible for the patient to maintain the performance when testing far lateral gaze on motility exam. It requires a great deal of effort to sustain volitional oscillations for more than a few seconds so it is helpful when attacks are noted to last only a few seconds. Oscillopsia is the sensation that the visual field is moving and is much more commonly described by patients with acquired nystagmus and nystagmoid eye movements. Its presence or absence on history, however, is not helpful in diagnosing voluntary nystagmoid eye movements. 16-month-old boy presents to your eye clinic because his parents noted his right eye "shaking" for the past month. Your exam shows fix, follow, intermittent maintain "FF(M)" vision OD and fix, follow, and maintain "FFM" vision OS. The pupil exam shows a trace APD OD. Motility is full and alignment is orthophoric based on alternate cover testing. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OD and -1.00 OS. External exam reveals a fine shimmering vertical nystagmus in the right eye with no nystagmus seen in the left eye. No head bobbing or torticollis is seen. Slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable. What is the next most appropriate step in the care of this patient? A.Prescribe glasses and follow-up in 3 months for re-evaluation B.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation C.Observe with repeat examination in 3 months D.Patch the left eye 6 hours daily and return in 3 month High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Monocular nystagmus in a child should immediately raise concerns for an optic nerve glioma. A monocular, small amplitude vertical nystagmus has been referred to as the Heimann- Bielschowsky phenomenon and may occur in association with any cause of decreased vision including amblyopia. This patient does have anisometropia which could cause amblyopia and account for his mild decrease in vision OD. The APD in the right eye is highly concerning for organic pathology, however. Severe amblyopia can result in a mild APD but in this situation organic pathology (such as a glioma) of the optic nerve, chiasm, or tract must be excluded. Spasmus nutans, a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding, can closely resemble Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans. The parents of a 4-year-old boy with torticollis and vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye since 1 year of age come to your clinic for a second opinion. The patient was diagnosed with spasmus nutans by another provider at presentation 3 years ago after a reportedly normal MRI. By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. His visual field is full to confrontation with finger count techniques, motility normal, and alignment orthophoric by alternate cover testing. The patient was uncooperative for pupillary testing so it was difficult to assess for an APD although his pupils reacted to light bilaterally. External exam confirms a monocular vertical shimmering nystagmus of the right eye and torticollis with a right head tilt. His penlight anterior segment exam is grossly normal and dilated fundus exam reveals trace pallor of the right optic nerve. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in both eyes. What is the next best step in the care of this patient? A.Order an MRI of the brain and orbits under sedation B.Reassure the parents and have the patient follow-up in one year C.Prescribe glasses and have the patient follow-up in one year D.Initiate patching for 6 hours daily in the left eye. Which of the following is NOT a recognized cause of downbeat nystagmus? A.Arnold-Chiari type I malformation B.Demyelination the cerebellum and/or medulla C.Migraine D.Magnesium deficiency High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: C Explanation: Downbeat nystagmus (DBN) is the result of abnormal drift of the eyes upward followed by a corrective downward fast saccade. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of congenital nystagmus? A.Presence of a null point B.Predominantly a conjugate, vertical nystagmus C.Manifests with either pendular or jerk nystagmus D.Intensifies with viewing of objects at distance High Yield: Yes Your Answer: D Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital nystagmus is a highly tested topic. question: Which of the following history and exam features are NOT helpful in distinguishing voluntary (or self-induced) nystagmoid movements from other involuntary forms of nystagmus and nystagmoid movements?

options.A: Associated facial grimacing and eyelid flutter

explanation: The most common functional neuro-ophthalmic complaints probably involve vision loss but functional or voluntary nystagmoid movements can present to your clinic as well. The diagnosis of volitional nystagmoid movements can usually be made easily in the clinic by looking for associated facial grimacing or eyelid flutter. Distracting the patient by having them perform tasks often breaks a cycle of oscillations. Usually the eye movements are low amplitude and associated with convergence movements so it is nearly impossible for the patient to maintain the performance when testing far lateral gaze on motility exam. It requires a great deal of effort to sustain volitional oscillations for more than a few seconds so it is helpful when attacks are noted to last only a few seconds. Oscillopsia is the sensation that the visual field is moving and is much more commonly described by patients with acquired nystagmus and nystagmoid eye movements. Your exam shows fix, follow, intermittent maintain "FF(M)" vision OD and fix, follow, and maintain "FFM" vision OS. The pupil exam shows a trace APD OD. Motility is full and alignment is orthophoric based on alternate cover testing. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OD and -1.00 OS. External exam reveals a fine shimmering vertical nystagmus in the right eye with no nystagmus seen in the left eye. No head bobbing or torticollis is seen. Slit lamp exam and fundus exam is unremarkable. What is the next most appropriate step in the care of this patient? The patient was diagnosed with spasmus nutans by another provider at presentation 3 years ago after a reportedly normal MRI. By matching Allen pictures, the patient has 20/100 vision OD and 20/50 vision OS. His visual field is full to confrontation with finger count techniques, motility normal, and alignment orthophoric by alternate cover testing. The patient was uncooperative for pupillary testing so it was difficult to assess for an APD although his pupils reacted to light bilaterally. question: What is the standard "cycle" time required for periodic alternating nystagmus to pass from the static (nystagmus free) phase through two nystagmus phases in different directions and back to a static phase?
explanation: Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) is a form of bilateral, horizontal jerk nystagmus that alternates fast phase directions following a reliable time cycle (usually 2-4 minutes). The cycle begins with a static phase devoid of nystagmus and is followed by crescendo then decrescendo jerk nystagmus to one side. A return to the static phase occurs after which there is a crescendo / decrescendo jerk nystagmus to the opposite side. The cycle then terminates with another static phase. PAN may be congenital or acquired. When acquired it is usually caused by posterior fossa pathology of the brainstem or cerebellum (especially the vermis of the cerebellum). Because of the reliability of the short cycle and the importance of diagnosis, all patients with horizontal jerk nystagmus should be observed for a minimum of 2 minutes to ensure that the diagnosis of PAN is not missed. One of the greatest concerns in missing the diagnosis of PAN is that the null point in patients with PAN can alternate depending on the direction of the jerk nystagmus. For this reason, Kestenbaum surgery or Kestenbaum variants used to shift the null point to primary gaze should be avoided in these patients unless it is clear that the patient always maintains the same null point throughout the PAN cycle. question: Which of the following descriptive terms of nystagmus is correctly defined below?

options.A: Dissociated nystagmus: the amplitude of oscillations differs in each eye
options.B: Disconjugate nystagmus: nystagmus in one eye only
options.C: Null point: the point of gaze where there is no nystagmus
options.D: Disjunctive: nystagmus in one eye only

explanation: Nystagmus terminology can be confusing and standardized tests may take advantage of that confusion. Dissociated nystagmus is a nystagmus where the amplitude of the wave form differs in each eye (for instance the nystagmus is much more pronounced in the right eye than the left). Disconjugate nystagmus (also known as disjunctive nystagmus) occurs when the direction of nystagmus differs between two eyes (for instance a right beating nystagmus in the right eye and a left beating nystagmus in the left eye). A null point is the point of gaze where the nystagmus is least severe. The nystagmus is usually not absent in the null point but dampened. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of spasmus nutans? A.Resolution after 1-2 years B.Onset within the first 2 years of life C.High amplitude horizontal, vertical, or rotary nystagmus D.Abnormal head posturing and nodding High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Spasmus nutans is a benign self-limited disorder of high frequency low amplitude nystagmus with associated torticollis and head nodding. The nystagmus is frequently referred to as "shimmering" due to its high frequency low amplitude nature. The nystagmus is usually horizontal and bilateral although it may be unilateral, vertical, or rotary. It usually presents within the first 2 years of life and then resolves within 1-2 years. Aside from an increased incidence of strabismus, spasmus nutans is not associated with other neurological deficits or diseases. Spasmus nutans can closely resemble Heimann- Bielschowsky phenomenon and vice-versa so most clinicians (and the BCSC) suggest scanning all patients with spasmus nutans to rule out an anterior optic pathway glioma. A variety of links have been suggested by OQ users to show spasmus nutans. I believe this link to the University of Utah's NOVEL page is probably the best example and also provides excellent additional didactic narration regarding spasmus nutans. LINK Convergence retraction nystagmus is NOT associated with which of the following exam findings? A.Bilateral superior eyelid retraction B.Lateral gaze palsy C.Abnormal convergence D.Pupillary light-near dissociation High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Convergence-retraction nystagmus is one component of the dorsal midbrain syndrome (aka Parinaud's syndrome) and is marked by abnormal co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on attempted up-gaze. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is most easily elicited by a holding a down going OKN drum or OKN strip in front of the patient. The patient will momentarily follow one target downward before a fast upward "catch-up" saccade occurs to find the next target. The convergence- retraction nystagmus occurs simultaneously with the attempted fast upward saccade. Other features of dorsal midbrain syndrome include limitation of conjugate upgaze, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation (meaning the pupils constrict more to near than to light), and bilateral superior eyelid retraction (Collier's sign). Other findings associated with dorsal midbrain syndrome but not major components include convergence spasm, convergence insufficiency / paresis, accommodative insufficiency, and skew deviation. Rarely do all of the features of dorsal midbrain syndrome occur in the same patient; the defining and most commonly exhibited characteristic of the syndrome is upgaze palsy. A 20-year-old male comes to see you for vertical binocular diplopia and difficulty focusing after removal of a cerebellar tumor. The relevant portion of his exam is shown in the video below. What is the best term for this patient’s horizontal eye movements? ( video missing ) A.Volitional nystagmus B.Horizontal jerk nystagmus C.Square wave jerks D.Ocular flutter High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient with a clear cause for cerebellar dysfunction shows exam findings typical of square wave jerks (SWJs). For those astute observers, the patient also had a right hypertropia (which can barely be appreciated in the video) related to a skew deviation following his cerebellar tumor excision. SWJs are a type of saccadic intrusion. Unlike nystagmus, square wave jerks lack a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees) although amplitudes can be greater than 5 degrees in which case the name “macrosquare wave jerks” may be used. Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or "intersaccadic interval") and then a quick return to fixation. That intersaccadic interval is characteristically 200 msec when mapped with eye movement tracings. Interestingly the term square wave jerk arises from the square waveform on eye movement tracings (see reference links below for examples). SWJs can be physiologic but when there are more than 9 per minute it is typically pathologic. Common causes include cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and supranuclear palsy. An astute eye care provider will look for signs and inquire about symptoms of Parkinsonism in any patient exhibiting frequent SWJs. If there are additional concerns for Parkinsonism then referral to a Neurologist with experience in movement disorders is indicated. While it might be easy to mistake abundant SWJs for horizontal pendular nystagmus, the intersaccadic interval (time where eyes fixate without moving) is seen only in SWJs. There is clearly no fast phase / slow phase present in this case so jerk nystagmus is not a consideration. Ocular flutter is a sustained horizontal saccadic intrusion without intersaccadic intervals and has a broad differential diagnosis identical to that of opsoclonus. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high- frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (but not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. References: 1. http://www.dizziness-and-balance.com/practice/nystagmus/SWJ.htm 2. http://www.neuroophthalmology.ca/textbook/e-figures/square-wave-jerks-waveforms What is the most accurate means to quantify the severity of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the clinic? A.The time required for release of the pupil upon swinging a light to the abnormal eye B.The speed and extent of reactivity of the pupil to light in the abnormal eye C.The visual acuity in the abnormal eye D.Neutral density filters High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Many clinicians do not quantify the severity of an APD in practice preferring instead to only document its presence. Some clinicians will comment on whether an APD is questionable, subtle, or brisk. Some clinicians will measure the severity of an APD by using neutral density filters. In a patient with a right APD, neutral density filters are held over the left eye starting with the least dense filter (usually 0.3 log units). The swinging flashlight test is then performed with the filter covering the left eye. If the right pupil still dilates immediately when the flashlight is swung from the left eye to the right eye then the APD is still present. The density of the filter over the left eye is increased to 0.6 log units and the swinging flashlight test is repeated. This continues until the APD has been "neutralized." If too strong of a filter is placed over the better eye then the APD will actually reverse. The density of the filter required to neutralize the APD defines the severity of the APD. The advantage of grading an APD is that it allows an additional objective means (along with visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields) to follow a patient for possible progression of optic nerve pathology. If only the presence of an APD is documented then it is impossible to know if the APD gets worse over time. Approximately what percentage of eyes affected by demyelinating optic neuritis demonstrate optic disc edema? A.35% B.55% C.75% D.95% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT) showed that most optic nerves (65%) in demyelinating optic neuritis were normal appearing. Also, the ONTT found that eyes with peripapillary optic nerve hemorrhages had a markedly reduced risk of developing multiple sclerosis compared to all eyes with optic neuritis. Which of the following types of nystagmus usually has a delayed onset presenting months to years following an inciting stroke of the brainstem? A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) (answer choice B) is a peculiar form of nystagmus with a cyclical transition of right beating to left beating jerk nystagmus. For a short period in the middle of the cycle there may be no apparent or minimal nystagmus and there can even be shift null points depending on where in the cycle the patient is. A complete PAN cycle usually lasts around 4 minutes. PAN may be acquired from a lesion of the cerebellum (particularly the nodulus or uvulua) or may be congenital. Acquired PAN often improves with baclofen (high yield testing point). Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) (answer choice C) is characterized by a slow drift down followed by a corrective fast saccade up. UBN localizes to the brainstem (typically the medulla) and the anterior cerebellar vermis. Common causes include thiamine deficiency (which often starts as UBN and transitions to DBN with time), demyelination, stroke, and cerebellar degeneration. See-saw nystagmus (SSN)(answer choice D) is characterized by rhythmic alternating of one eye elevating and incyclotorting while the other eye simultaneously depresses and excylotorts followed by the reverse movement. SSN is highly localizable to the midbrain and parasellar region. It is not unusual for SSN patients to exhibit bitemporal hemianopic field defects and bilateral optic atrophy because the parasellar lesion causing the nystagmus also results in disruption of the nearby visual pathways. Hence SSN is a rare example of when both nystagmus and visual field defects can be caused by one lesion.

Unlike nystagmus, square wave jerks lack a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees) although amplitudes can be greater than 5 degrees in which case the name “macrosquare wave jerks” may be used. Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or "intersaccadic interval") and then a quick return to fixation. That intersaccadic interval is characteristically 200 msec when mapped with eye movement tracings. Interestingly the term square wave jerk arises from the square waveform on eye movement tracings (see reference links below for examples). SWJs can be physiologic but when there are more than 9 per minute it is typically pathologic. Common causes include cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and supranuclear palsy. An astute eye care provider will look for signs and inquire about symptoms of Parkinsonism in any patient exhibiting frequent SWJs. If there are additional concerns for Parkinsonism then referral to a Neurologist with experience in movement disorders is indicated. While it might be easy to mistake abundant SWJs for horizontal pendular nystagmus, the intersaccadic interval (time where eyes fixate without moving) is seen only in SWJs. There is clearly no fast phase / slow phase present in this case so jerk nystagmus is not a consideration. Ocular flutter is a sustained horizontal saccadic intrusion without intersaccadic intervals and has a broad differential diagnosis identical to that of opsoclonus. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high- frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (but not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. References: 1. http://www.dizziness-and-balance.com/practice/nystagmus/SWJ.htm 2. http://www.neuroophthalmology.ca/textbook/e-figures/square-wave-jerks-waveforms What is the most accurate means to quantify the severity of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the clinic? A.The time required for release of the pupil upon swinging a light to the abnormal eye B.The speed and extent of reactivity of the pupil to light in the abnormal eye C.The visual acuity in the abnormal eye D.Neutral density filters High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Many clinicians do not quantify the severity of an APD in practice preferring instead to only document its presence. Some clinicians will comment on whether an APD is questionable, subtle, or brisk. Some clinicians will measure the severity of an APD by using neutral density filters. In a patient with a right APD, neutral density filters are held over the left eye starting with the least dense filter (usually 0.3 log units). The swinging flashlight test is then performed with the filter covering the left eye. If the right pupil still dilates immediately when the flashlight is swung from the left eye to the right eye then the APD is still present. The density of the filter over the left eye is increased to 0.6 log units and the swinging flashlight test is repeated. This continues until the APD has been "neutralized." If too strong of a filter is placed over the better eye then the APD will actually reverse. The density of the filter required to neutralize the APD defines the severity of the APD. The advantage of grading an APD is that it allows an additional objective means (along with visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields) to follow a patient for possible progression of optic nerve pathology. If only the presence of an APD is documented then it is impossible to know if the APD gets worse over time. Approximately what percentage of eyes affected by demyelinating optic neuritis demonstrate optic disc edema? A.35% B.55% C.75% D.95% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT) showed that most optic nerves (65%) in demyelinating optic neuritis were normal appearing. Also, the ONTT found that eyes with peripapillary optic nerve hemorrhages had a markedly reduced risk of developing multiple sclerosis compared to all eyes with optic neuritis. Which of the following types of nystagmus usually has a delayed onset presenting months to years following an inciting stroke of the brainstem? A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) (answer choice B) is a peculiar form of nystagmus with a cyclical transition of right beating to left beating jerk nystagmus. For a short period in the middle of the cycle there may be no apparent or minimal nystagmus and there can even be shift null points depending on where in the cycle the patient is. A complete PAN cycle usually lasts around 4 minutes. PAN may be acquired from a lesion of the cerebellum (particularly the nodulus or uvulua) or may be congenital. Acquired PAN often improves with baclofen (high yield testing point). Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) (answer choice C) is characterized by a slow drift down followed by a corrective fast saccade up. UBN localizes to the brainstem (typically the medulla) and the anterior cerebellar vermis. Common causes include thiamine deficiency (which often starts as UBN and transitions to DBN with time), demyelination, stroke, and cerebellar degeneration. See-saw nystagmus (SSN)(answer choice D) is characterized by rhythmic alternating of one eye elevating and incyclotorting while the other eye simultaneously depresses and excylotorts followed by the reverse movement. SSN is highly localizable to the midbrain and parasellar region. It is not unusual for SSN patients to exhibit bitemporal hemianopic field defects and bilateral optic atrophy because the parasellar lesion causing the nystagmus also results in disruption of the nearby visual pathways. Hence SSN is a rare example of when both nystagmus and visual field defects can be caused by one lesion.
